category.name: App Security
category.description: Application-layer threat modeling: authentication, sessions, data handling and third-party integrations.

lab.title: Retail Banking Transfers
lab.summary: A money-movement flow where a mobile app initiates transfers through a core banking system.
lab.businessContext: A retail bank is launching in-app transfers between customer accounts and to external payees.
lab.systemContext: A mobile client talks to an API gateway, which reaches an auth service, a transfers service, a core ledger and an external payments rail.

nodes.label: API Gateway
nodes.description: Public entry point for all mobile traffic

architectureIssues.title: No step-up authentication for high-value transfers
architectureIssues.description: Every transfer is authorised by the same access token regardless of amount or payee novelty. A stolen token moves any sum.
architectureIssues.hint: Does a £5 transfer to a saved payee deserve the same scrutiny as £50,000 to a new one?

architectureIssues.title: Gateway to transfers hop is unencrypted
architectureIssues.description: Transfer instructions cross from the edge into the regulated core over plain HTTP.
architectureIssues.hint: Compare this protocol with the one used to reach the ledger.

architectureIssues.title: No idempotency on transfer execution
architectureIssues.description: A retried or replayed request has nothing to deduplicate against, so the same instruction can debit an account twice.
architectureIssues.hint: What happens if the mobile app times out and the customer taps again?

architectureIssues.title: Audit events are writable by the service that creates them
architectureIssues.description: The transfers service writes its own audit trail with no append-only guarantee, so a compromise can erase its own tracks.
architectureIssues.hint: Who can edit the record of what happened?

architectureIssues.title: No described validation of external payee details
architectureIssues.description: Payee account details flow to the external rail with no stated verification or confirmation-of-payee check.
architectureIssues.hint: How would the customer know the money is going where they think?

threats.title: Stolen access token authorises unlimited transfers
threats.description: A token lifted from a compromised device or intercepted session can move any amount to any payee, because nothing re-authenticates the customer at the point of payment.
threats.learnerExplanation: Authentication at login is not authorisation at payment time.

threats.title: Replayed transfer instruction debits twice
threats.description: Without an idempotency key a retried request executes the same debit again, creating real financial loss and a reconciliation problem.
threats.learnerExplanation: In money movement, at-least-once delivery without idempotency means duplicate debits.

threats.title: Interception of transfer instructions on the edge-to-core hop
threats.description: Plain HTTP across a trust boundary lets an attacker on that segment read balances and alter amounts or payees in flight.
threats.learnerExplanation: A boundary crossing without transport security is an interception point.

threats.title: Attacker erases their own audit trail
threats.description: Because the transfers service can rewrite the audit store, a compromise of that service destroys the evidence needed to investigate it.
threats.learnerExplanation: An audit log the attacker can edit is not an audit log.

threats.title: Authorised push payment fraud to an attacker-controlled payee
threats.description: With no confirmation-of-payee, a socially engineered customer sends funds to an account that is not who they believe it is.
threats.learnerExplanation: Some fraud needs no technical compromise at all.

mitigations.title: Step-up authentication on risk signals
mitigations.description: Require re-authentication or a second factor for high-value amounts, new payees and unusual devices.

mitigations.title: Mutual TLS on every trust boundary crossing
mitigations.description: Encrypt and mutually authenticate edge-to-core traffic so the segment cannot be read or altered.

mitigations.title: Idempotency keys on transfer execution
mitigations.description: Require a client-supplied key per instruction and store it, so a replay returns the original result instead of debiting again.

mitigations.title: Append-only audit store with separate credentials
mitigations.description: Write audit events to storage the application cannot update or delete, under a different identity.

mitigations.title: Confirmation of payee before settlement
mitigations.description: Verify the payee name against the destination account and warn the customer on a mismatch.

mitigations.title: Enable TLS on the public endpoint
mitigations.description: A baseline control that protects the internet-facing hop, already present here and not the gap.

mitigations.title: CAPTCHA on the login form
mitigations.description: Slows automated credential stuffing but does nothing about any of the design flaws in this flow.

threatMitigations.explanation: Re-authenticating at payment time makes a stolen token insufficient on its own.
A stored key makes the second execution a no-op that returns the first result.
Encrypts and authenticates the hop, removing the interception point.
Separate credentials and append-only semantics stop a compromised service rewriting history.
Surfacing a name mismatch gives the customer the chance to stop before sending.

releaseGuidance.rationale: Two of the findings are critical in a regulated money-movement flow: any stolen token can move unlimited funds, and a retried request can debit a customer twice. Both cause direct, irreversible financial loss to real customers, and the missing audit integrity means the bank could not reconstruct what happened afterwards. Unlike a contained bug, step-up auth and idempotency are structural changes to the payment path. 'Ship with conditions' is defensible only if the launch is limited to low-value transfers between the customer's own accounts.
suggestedConditions: Implement step-up authentication for high-value and new-payee transfers.
Add idempotency keys to the transfer execution path.
Move audit events to an append-only store with separate credentials.
Enable mTLS on the gateway-to-core hop.
